Goto Survey Viewer

A portable 3D viewer and annotator

After processing the data I collected for Rijkswaterstaat, I realized they would need a way to view and annotate the models in order to make use of the work we had collected. Rijkswaterstaat didn't have a dedicated data professional for this project so I knew that they would get more mileage from the work if I included some helpful tools built and packaged with their dataset. It's easier than ever to build custom software, so I included a 3D viewer and annotator to deliver along with the final report.

The viewer launches alongside the final report and allows users to explore the scans, selecting the terminal and scan they want to inspect and using camera controls to rotate, pan, and zoom. The archive contains approximately 14,695 m² of horizontal footprint reconstructed from 35,611 photographs and spread across seven scans. It's almost 900 GB, not a small dataset, so having a central place to inspect and review the scan data will extend the reach of the data. This will allow officials at Rijkswaterstaat, who don't have data expertise, to make use of the data from this report and extend the impact of my work.

Label and review

Rijkswaterstaat commissioned this work because they were interested in preventing further degradation of the reef surrounding the Goto terminal. Before its bankruptcy and closure, BOPEC had mismanaged the disposal of industrial waste at the terminal, and there is a substantial amount of debris from the terminal built up over the years. This scan was to serve as a baseline to establish what historical debris was present when CBET took over management of the pier. Finding and labeling the metal waste is important to the project’s broader goal of reducing the impact of this pier system on the reef, so I built a simple annotator in the viewer that allows for the easy generation of reports identifying the current debris.

Inspecting the source data photographs

The summary 3D models are rendered from high-quality depth maps in Agisoft Metashape, but model geometry and orthomosaic stitching are never perfect. Occasionally, an object of interest might be difficult to ascertain from the reconstructions. In some cases, it's helpful to return to the source photographs to inspect what the camera saw at that point. But with 35 thousand photographs across seven scans, it's not feasible to find the original photographs that contributed to the reconstruction point.

The viewer allows users to select points on the surface of the model and review galleries of the source images where the camera had a field of view that contains the point. Obstruction and distance mean this can still match photos that don't clearly show the object, but it reduces the sample set to something easily reviewable. This improves traceability of the source data by making it easier for a nontechnical professional to review what the camera saw and ascertain what's actually in the scan.

Georeferencing and alignment

The scan reconstruction required the manual alignment of the 4 scans for Terminal A and the 3 scans for Terminal B into the same model space. In the field, I had allowed for substantial overlap between each scan to facilitate reconstruction of the multiscan models. Automatic alignment in Agisoft failed, likely due to the size of the scan or the complexity of the model, and hardware limitations and scaling constraints made reconstruction of the full model from the combined photosets impractical. So in Agisoft, I selected 6 to 8 points on each scan that overlapped another, and then imported the scans into the same space and aligned them with marker-based alignment. This allowed the viewer to switch between the scans and display multiple scans from the same model seamlessly.

Georeferencing was completed by attaching GPS coordinates taken from the surface to points on the model. The piers of the terminals made for easy reference points, and 69 GPS coordinates taken at the surface were combined into 12 reference points aligned to the bottom. These were added into the models, allowing them to be aligned in a georeferenced space, and will be useful for returning to specific points in the field for future observations or work.

Area & depth

Model scale was established with eight fixed-length markers distributed across each scan. These meter-long markers were then set in Agisoft as scale bars, allowing for the estimation of debris size. The total scanned area was estimated after model scaling by measuring the 2D footprint of each scan projected onto a plane, with overlapping areas subtracted from the total. These area totals do not show how evenly a site was photographed, and the deeper sections of the model and the edges can distort the usable area coverage estimates. The report compares the full footprint with areas supported by at least 10 or 20 cameras, identifying stronger photographic coverage. These boundaries distinguish the reconstructed extent from areas with stronger photographic support.

Coverage maps retain holes and fragments and count overlap once per terminal. Structures, shadows, water conditions, and access constrained capture. Camera support describes available observations, rather than measuring accuracy.

Model-derived depths appear alongside field depths recorded at scale-bar centres, helping reviewers interpret the vertical structure and its reference measurements. These references also explain the limits of the depth measurements available for interpreting the model.

Portability

The survey archive includes the application and runtime for offline inspection. Recipients make the delivery folder available offline, then open a launcher to use the report, viewer, and debris gallery without installing Node.js. The report, 3D viewer, and gallery run in a browser with no connection to an online application required.

Three.js and a 3D Tiles renderer display the scene. A local Node.js server streams model tiles and photo thumbnails from indexed archives, avoiding full extraction or loading of entire datasets.

Camera metadata links models to source JPGs. Separate JSON files preserve labelled positions and views for report links, giving recipients an overview, photographic evidence, and observations they can revisit.

Tools

Viewer source code on GitHub

The scans were captured using a twin-camera setup, described in more detail on the expedition page. The scans were processed in Agisoft Metashape using the baseline pipeline batch processing project built during the Bonaire Baseline scans. The actual reconstruction work is handled using Agisoft Metashape. OpenAI’s Codex was used extensively for the development of the viewer code.

Connecting fieldwork, research, and design

My work brings together experience in product design, underwater research, and scientific publishing. I'm interested in ecological change, deep time, and how people participate in thriving ecosystems across generations.
